articles.title: ‘Greater Israel’: Christian Zionism’s role in US policy
articles.summary: Israel, the US, Christian Zionism and the search for Armageddon.
articles.body:
A sermon becomes a map. A map becomes policy. And policy becomes land taken, homes emptied and borders redrawn. ‘Greater Israel’: How Christian Zionism Became Policy – a 22-minute Al Jazeera Originals documentary directed by Awad Joumaa – traces how a centuries-old biblical idea travelled from English fringe pulpits to the heart of US politics, and from prophecy into the machinery of modern power. Blending archival footage and AI-assisted visuals, the film explores a question that no longer belongs only to theologians or historians: what happens when a religious vision of territory is backed by votes, money, military infrastructure and state policy?

In a megachurch in San Antonio, Texas, Pastor John Hagee reads the map aloud. God, he says, promised the Jewish people “one-half of modern-day Egypt, all of Israel, all of Lebanon, all of Syria, all of Jordan, all of Kuwait, and three-fourths of Saudi Arabia”.

This is not a negotiation, he tells his congregation.

“God’s not saying, ‘Let’s make a deal’. He’s saying, ‘This is the deal.'”

Hagee is not a fringe preacher. He is the founder of Christians United for Israel, or CUFI, which claims more than 10 million members and has become one of the most powerful pro-Israel organisations in the United States.

The film explores a world in which scripture is read as geography, geography becomes entitlement, and entitlement is carried to Washington, DC, through lobbying, elections and policy.

Christian Zionism is often described as a belief system. In the United States, it is also a political force.

White evangelical Protestants account for roughly 13 percent of the US adult population, about 35 million people, and most identify as Republican. Their views on Israel are unusually firm. A 2018 LifeWay Research survey for Chosen People Ministries found that 80 percent of evangelicals believed the creation of Israel in 1948 was a fulfilment of biblical prophecy that would bring about Christ’s return. Roughly two-thirds said the modern state of Israel was an outgrowth of the biblical covenant.

That belief translates into votes. Pew Research Center’s analysis of the 2024 election found that 82 percent of white evangelical voters backed Donald Trump in the recent midterms, the highest support of any religious group.

It also shapes attitudes towards war. The Chicago Council on Global Affairs found in 2024 that 64 percent of white evangelicals said Israel’s actions in Gaza were justified, roughly double the share of Americans overall, while 60 percent opposed cutting US military aid to Israel.

“The bedrock of support for the State of Israel is there because American evangelicals think it will bring Jesus back quicker,” former evangelical insider Frank Schaeffer says in Al Jazeera‘s 2024 documentary Praying for Armageddon . “And without the Republican bedrock evangelical voter, no Republican anywhere in America, for any office, gets elected. We don’t want peace, we being evangelicals. We want Armageddon.”

The theology is preached from pulpits. The machinery runs through donations, lobbying and tax-exempt advocacy.

The International Fellowship of Christians and Jews says it has raised more than $3.6bn since 1983, with 92 percent of its donors identifying as Christian. Mother Jones, the US publication, has traced how Christian Zionist networks have channelled money into Israeli causes, including organisations linked to settlement expansion in the occupied West Bank.

CUFI’s political arm is smaller in dollar terms but influential in access. OpenSecrets records $679,410 in federal lobbying spending by CUFI Action Fund in 2025.

God’s not saying, 'Let’s make a deal.' He’s saying, 'This is the deal' by Pastor John Hagee, founder, Christians United for Israel

God’s not saying, 'Let’s make a deal.' He’s saying, 'This is the deal'

by Pastor John Hagee, founder, Christians United for Israel

The Congressional Research Service, in its 2024 overview of US aid to Israel, notes that both AIPAC and CUFI “express unequivocal support for US security assistance to Israel”.

Inside Washington, the influence is structural. Ralph Drollinger’s Capitol Ministries – which advocates a “ Biblical case for defending Israel ” – runs weekly Bible studies attended by members of Congress. During the first Trump administration, it convened a cabinet-level Bible study. The theology is not only in churches; it is in the room where power gathers.

The Christian Zionist map of Israel itself comes from scripture. In Genesis 15, a part of the Torah and Old Testament, God promises Abraham’s descendants land “from the river of Egypt to the great river, the Euphrates”. For Christian Zionists and some Israeli ultranationalists, that passage is not a metaphor. It is a title deed.

In February 2026, the US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, sat with independent broadcaster Tucker Carlson as Carlson read out the biblical passage describing land “from the Euphrates to the Nile”. Asked whether Israel had a right to all of it, Huckabee replied : “It would be fine if they took it all.”

Such a vision is not new. As Professor John Mearsheimer of the University of Chicago notes in this film, Israel’s first prime minister, David Ben-Gurion, wrote in 1918 of a Greater Israel that would include all of historical Palestine, parts of southern Lebanon, southern Syria, the east bank of the Jordan and the Sinai Peninsula. It was not merely a fringe fantasy. It was part of the strategic imagination of early Zionism.

That imagination survives in the settler movement. Daniella Weiss, one of the most prominent leaders of the settlement enterprise, has insisted southern Lebanon is part of the vision of Greater Israel. In her words, “It is part of it. All of it, even parts of Syria, part of Iraq, part of Iran. It’s huge.”

Israel’s far-right finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, has framed the claim in overtly religious language, praying publicly for “the expansion of the borders of the land of Israel for the complete redemption and for the building of the Temple”. In the Knesset, he has also declared that “there is no such thing as a Palestinian people”.

In 2017, Smotrich published what he called his “Decisive Plan”, arguing that the conflict should be resolved, not through Palestinian statehood, but through Israeli victory. Palestinians, he wrote, would face a choice: accept permanent Israeli sovereignty, emigrate, or resist and be defeated. The document gave ideological form to what is now visible on the ground: annexation without the word annexation.

Syria: The buffer zone becomes occupied ground

Syria shows how Israel has used the language of “security” to move further east.

After the collapse of the Bashar al-Assad government in December 2024, Israel moved beyond the occupied Golan Heights into the demilitarised buffer zone that had separated Israeli and Syrian forces since a 1974 disengagement agreement. Al Jazeera has reported that Israel captured about 400 square kilometres, or 155 square miles, of Syrian territory beyond the western Golan Heights it has occupied since 1967.

The move was presented by Israel as defensive and temporary . But the language of temporary security has a long history in the region. The occupied Golan Heights itself was seized in 1967 and later annexed by Israel in a move rejected internationally. Decades later, it remains under Israeli control.

Al Jazeera has also reported on Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu appearing with Israeli troops in occupied territory in southern Syria, a visit that angered Damascus and raised questions over whether any future deal was possible.

The Syrian case is crucial because it turns biblical geography into military geography. The Greater Israel idea speaks of borders stretching north and east. Israeli policy speaks of buffer zones, demilitarisation and strategic depth. For Syrians living under the shadow of Israeli military expansion, the distinction may matter less than the fact of land taken.

South Lebanon: Occupation by another name

Israel’s invasion of southern Lebanon may well mark another move towards creating Greater Israel.

Israel occupied parts of southern Lebanon from 1982 until its withdrawal in 2000. But the border never became quiet, and after the latest war, Israel’s presence has again moved beyond episodic strikes. According to Al Jazeera reporting, Israeli forces have destroyed dozens of villages in southern Lebanon over the last 100 days, while attacks have continued despite ceasefire frameworks.

Al Jazeera has reported that Israel is currently occupying dozens of villages in southern Lebanon and preventing thousands of people from returning home. In one investigation, residents and officials described how Israeli attacks have damaged water infrastructure , deepening the conditions that make return impossible.

Another report showed more than 100 towns and villages across Lebanon were placed under forced displacement orders during the war, extending far beyond the immediate border area.

This is how a supposedly temporary security zone could become a political fact. A village is evacuated. A road is closed. Water networks are destroyed. The army remains. Residents cannot return. On paper, the border may still exist. On the ground, life is reorganised around Israeli military control, and eventually, geography is remade.

Borders are not redrawn only by tanks. They are also redrawn by permits, checkpoints, bypass roads, military zones and demolition orders.

In the occupied West Bank, more than 60 percent of the territory lies in Area C, under direct Israeli civil and military control. Palestinian construction is heavily restricted, while illegal Israeli outposts are often retroactively authorised. The separation wall, which the International Court of Justice ruled illegal in 2004 where it runs inside occupied territory, helped turn geography into policy.

The same logic appears across the occupied Palestinian territory: land is fragmented, movement is controlled and Palestinian life is made administratively conditional. What looks on a map like one territory becomes, in practice, a system of islands.

UN Special Rapporteur Francesca Albanese has repeatedly warned that the destruction of Palestinian life in Gaza and the occupied territory is also a test of the international legal order. “What is lost in Palestine,” she told the UN Human Rights Council, “will be lost to us all.”

The pattern is visible beyond Palestine, too: enter on security grounds, build infrastructure, normalise the presence, and let the map change quietly.

Iraq sits awkwardly inside the Greater Israel imagination. The Euphrates, named in Genesis 15:18 as the eastern boundary of the promised land, runs through it. But the major strategists and ideologues driving the Greater Israel project did not usually speak of annexing Baghdad. Their stated aim was different: to break Iraq’s power.

In 1982, Oded Yinon, a former Israeli foreign ministry official, published A Strategy for Israel in the 1980s in Kivunim, a journal of the World Zionist Organization. He described Iraq as Israel’s greatest strategic threat and argued that it should be dissolved into three entities: a Shia state in the south, a Sunni state in the centre and a Kurdish state in the north. The fragmentation of Iraq, he wrote, was “guaranteed” as a strategic goal.

Fourteen years later, A Clean Break: A New Strategy for Securing the Realm, a 1996 policy paper prepared for Netanyahu by a study group led by Richard Perle – a Reagan-era Pentagon official who would go on to chair George W Bush’s Defense Policy Board, Douglas Feith – later Undersecretary of Defense for Policy, 2001-2005, and David Wurmser – later Middle East adviser to Vice President Dick Cheney, named “removing Saddam Hussein from power in Iraq” as “an important Israeli strategic objective in its own right”. All three authors entered the George W Bush administration in senior national security roles in the run-up to the 2003 invasion of Iraq.

There’s no evidence that the idea of a Greater Israel played any role in the Bush administration’s motivation for the Iraq war. But Pastor Hagee from the San Antonio church was clear: He called the Iraq war “the beginning of the end” and “the gateway to the Apocalypse”.

So Iraq’s role in the Greater Israel worldview is not simply territorial. It is strategic. A unified, powerful Arab state east of the Jordan River is a threat; a fragmented Iraq is an opportunity.

This messianic strand did not begin in Congress. It reaches back to 17th-century English Puritan preachers who believed the Jews had to return to the Holy Land before Christ could return. That belief was carried into Anglo-American Protestant culture long before the creation of Israel.

Long before the Balfour Declaration, American Christian Zionists were already lobbying presidents. In 1891, the Methodist lay preacher William Eugene Blackstone submitted a petition to President Benjamin Harrison calling for Palestine to be restored to the Jewish people. The “ Blackstone Memorial ” was signed by leading US politicians, businessmen and religious figures, making it one of the earliest organised Christian Zionist interventions in US politics.

The historian Regina Sharif identifies the hinge as Woodrow Wilson. After Wilson’s endorsement of Zionism, she argues, every American president who followed aligned, in one form or another, with the Zionist project.

Public opinion in the United States is now moving in the opposite direction to policy. A Pew Research Center survey published in April 2026 found that 60 percent of Americans now hold an unfavourable view of Israel, with the share saying “very unfavourable” rising from 10 percent in 2022 to 28 percent in 2026. The sharpest shifts are among younger Americans, including young Republicans.

A December 2025 IMEU Policy Project poll, conducted by YouGov, found that 51 percent of Republicans under 45 would prefer a 2028 presidential candidate who reduces US weapons shipments to Israel, while only 27 percent wanted shipments maintained or increased.

This suggests the political coalition that made Christian Zionist influence so formidable may no longer be as stable as it once appeared. The policy machine is still moving. But the electorate beneath it is beginning to shift.

Behind the slogans are villages with names.

In the South Hebron Hills, the herding community of Khirbet Zanuta, emptied under settler violence in late 2023, has watched repeated attempts to return blocked by demolitions and military closures, according to the Israeli rights group B’Tselem. In the same period, the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) recorded the displacement of more than 2,400 Palestinians in the occupied West Bank by settler violence and demolitions in 2024 alone, the highest annual figure on record. In 2026 so far, nearly 2,150 people have been displaced, per OCHA.

In southern Lebanon, the same story is written through damaged villages, destroyed infrastructure and families unable to return. In Syria, it is written through new military positions beyond the occupied Golan Heights. In Gaza, it is written through the destruction of homes, hospitals, universities and farmland.

The map is often discussed in abstractions: borders, prophecy, security, redemption. But every line moved on that map passes through homes, fields, schools, roads and cemeteries. Every grand theory is lived by ordinary people as expulsion, bombardment, closure or erasure.

For all the talk of prophecy and God’s will, maps do not move by themselves. Settlements do not build themselves. Bombs do not fall from heaven on their own.

What this film shows is a project assembled out of policy, money and votes: a creed translated into lobbying, appropriations, military infrastructure and lines on a map.

This is not ancient theology. It is present-day policy. Israeli bulldozers are clearing Palestinian homes in Masafer Yatta. Israeli forces are holding ground in southern Lebanon. Israel has moved deeper into Syrian territory beyond the Golan. And in Washington, religious language continues to influence political permission.

The sermon, the speech and the bulldozer are no longer separate stories. They are the same story.

articles.title: MPs urge Labour ministers to get on with trophy hunting ban
articles.summary: It has been over two years since Labour promised to ban imports of the parts of animals hunted for sport.
articles.body:
The government has been accused of dragging its feet on its manifesto promise to ban the import of hunting trophies.

Labour pledged at the 2024 general election to outlaw bringing the parts of animals killed by hunters for sport, such as heads or horns, into the UK.

But it has so far failed to bring a bill enacting the ban to Parliament, and in the two years since the election more than 40 import permits have been granted for hunting trophies.

Speaking during a debate on the subject, Environment Minister Jenny Riddell-Carpenter insisted the government was still committed to a ban and a bill would be delivered "when parliamentary time allows".

Labour MP Clive Efford, who had proposed Wednesday's Westminster Hall debate, said the minister's promise "really is not good enough".

"Who is the government afraid of?" he asked, arguing that only a "tiny minority of people" opposed the ban.

He continued: "This issue has been debated widely, over a great many years; there is not much more that we can learn from either side of the argument - this is the time that the government have to act and move forwards."

A ban was first proposed by the Conservative government in 2019, and in 2022 a bill implementing a ban was passed by MPs but ran out of time in the House of Lords.

Conservative MP Henry Smith, who sponsored that bill, accused peers of using "parliamentary devices" to block its passage into law.

During Wednesday's debate, several MPs urged the government to restart the process by introducing a fresh bill to Parliament.

Efford said: "Trophy hunting is not about conservation, it does not resolve issues of wildlife-human conflict, and it does not bring economic benefits to rural areas —certainly not in the way that tourism can.

"Local people have been attacked, their land stolen and their human rights abused. Private companies are stealing their homelands. Britain should not be accommodating this industry."

Labour's Rachael Maskell also called for a ban, but said the government could, in the meantime, make it illegal to advertise safari hunting and make it a criminal offence for UK residents to "celebrate their kill" by posting images on social media.

Labour MP Irene Campbell said she found it "upsetting" that hunting trophies could still be exported from the UK, pointing to an instance of a Scottish stag head being exported to Zimbabwe.

DUP MP Jim Shannon said the flow of hunting trophies coming into the country was continuing at "nearly two dozen a year while the government drag their feet".

Addressing the minister, he said: "I ask her to give us a timescale, give us a date and tell us when [the ban] will happen."

Conservative Roger Gale criticised those who hunted the animals, saying: "A yellow streak runs right through those people and they are revolting."

More than one MP suggested that the government was being pressured by the US not to introduce a ban.

Earlier this year, The Telegraph reported that Doug Burgum, the US interior secretary, wrote to the UK government arguing: "Legal, well-regulated hunting – particularly trophy hunting – plays a vital role in supporting healthy wildlife populations, restoring habitat and supporting local economies."

Responding to MPs, Riddell-Carpenter said the government remained committed to banning "the import of hunting trophies from species of conservation concern".

"Our aim is clear: to introduce the bill at the earliest opportunity and within this Parliament," she said, although she declined repeated invitations from MPs to set out a more specific timetable.

Opponents of the ban argue that it would undermine local economies and reduce the amount of money that could be spent on conservation projects.

The Community Leaders Network, a group of rural representatives from countries in southern Africa, argues that regulated hunting helps pay for rangers and wildlife management.

"In practice, a ban could do the opposite of what it intends: less funding can mean fewer patrols, more poaching, poorer habitat management, and ultimately less wildlife," it says.

An Oxford University report from 2024 concluded that a ban would not ease pressure on threatened species, and said around 79% of imports to the UK between 2015 and 2021 had came from countries where hunted species were "stable, increasing or abundant".

Currently it is legal to bring hunting trophies into the UK, as long as there is a permit to do so.

The government has said permits are only issued when "strict conditions" have been met, including demonstrating that their import "will not have a detrimental effect on the conservation status of the species".

Between July 2024 and September 2026, the government issued permits for 41 imports including 21 African elephants, four hippos, five lions, a leopard and a giraffe.

articles.title: More than 1,800 Italian schools targeted by new hoax bomb alerts
articles.summary: The latest warnings come amid rising concerns ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠in Europe about hybrid warfare threats.
articles.body:
⁠More than 1,800 ⁠schools in Italy were sent emails containing bomb threats on Thursday, the government said, a day after some 6,300 schools received similar alerts .

Many schools closed immediately after receiving the latest warnings, causing widespread disruption as parents rushed to collect their children.

Police in Rome said “there was nothing to substantiate” the threats.

Like Wednesday’s emails, the messages were reportedly signed by “Mikhail Andropov”, who presented himself as the “leader of the Vilayat of ⁠⁠⁠⁠Misoginistan”, according to Italy’s Ansa news agency.

The same purported author claimed responsibility for email bomb threats sent last week to newsrooms in Ireland and Bulgaria .

Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni summoned opposition leaders for talks on how to deal with similar incidents.

Meloni’s office said “buildings should not be evacuated in the absence of concrete elements beyond the mere receipt of a mass email that would suggest a genuine danger exists”, adding that it would instruct schools to act accordingly.

Authorities in Scotland, Northern Ireland and the Republic of Ireland said many schools had received similar threatening emails from abroad on Wednesday, but classified them as hoaxes and allowed classes to continue.

Opposition parties have accused Meloni of prioritising spending on conventional military equipment while neglecting what they say are ‌more ‌pressing cyberthreats.

“We need stronger coordination among the bodies responsible for cybersecurity, and we have proposed shifting part of the available resources towards cyberdefences,” said Elly Schlein, the leader of the main opposition Democratic Party.

The latest security alert came amid rising concerns ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠in Europe about hybrid warfare threats , which have targeted supermarkets, blood banks, air traffic and TV broadcasters.

On Tuesday, France summoned Iran’s ambassador after accusing Tehran of a cyberattack that disabled refrigerators in hundreds of supermarkets.⁠ Tehran rejected the French accusations as “baseless” and “hostile”.

Some European officials suspect Russia of orchestrating the campaign in countries supporting Ukraine after Moscow’s full-scale invasion. Russia denies the accusation and describes it as a smear campaign.

articles.title: We crossed the Rubicon with Iran, so we can’t stop halfway
articles.summary: A three-pronged strategy of diplomacy, sanctions and military force could keep Iran from rebuilding its missiles, drones and nuclear program.
articles.body: America has crossed the Rubicon with Iran. There is no going back to the world that existed before this war, no matter how much we might wish otherwise. We have attacked Iran’s military infrastructure, inflicted enormous damage on its economy and demonstrated that the United States is prepared to use overwhelming force. Now, at precisely the moment when we have gained the upper hand, Washington seems increasingly preoccupied with how quickly we can declare victory, bring down gasoline prices and move on. That would be a terrible mistake. The question is whether America is about to squander the military advantage it has gained over Iran. The answer depends on whether we understand the difference between stopping a war and achieving the objectives for which we fought it. FINISH THE JOB: WHY A HALF WAR WITH IRAN IS THE MOST DANGEROUS OUTCOME We need to be clear about the regime we are dealing with. The Islamic Republic is not simply another country with which we have disagreements over trade, borders or diplomatic recognition. Since 1979, hostility toward America and Israel has been woven into the regime’s revolutionary ideology. That is not a judgment about the Iranian people, many of whom want nothing more than a normal life. It is a judgment about the government that has ruled them for nearly half a century. Look at the history. In 1979, Iranian revolutionaries seized our embassy and held 52 Americans hostage for 444 days. In 1983, Hezbollah, which Iran helped create and arm, carried out the Beirut Marine barracks bombing that killed 241 American servicemen. In 1994, the bombing of the AMIA Jewish community center in Buenos Aires killed 85 people; an Argentine court subsequently held Iran responsible and concluded that Hezbollah carried out the attack. In 2011, American authorities uncovered an Iranian-linked plot to assassinate the Saudi ambassador in a Washington restaurant, potentially killing innocent Americans. We do not need to occupy the country, install a new government or demand a surrender ceremony in Tehran. We need to make it exceedingly difficult for the regime to rebuild the capabilities that threaten America, Israel and our allies. These were not isolated misunderstandings that could have been resolved over coffee. They occurred across decades, under Republican and Democratic administrations, during periods of confrontation and diplomatic engagement. Iran has repeatedly demonstrated a willingness to use terrorism, proxies and intimidation to advance its interests. Its leaders have called for Israel’s elimination while building the military capabilities to threaten it. Can we negotiate with this regime? Of course. We have to. But we should understand what those negotiations can realistically accomplish. I do not believe we are going to negotiate the Islamic Republic into becoming a responsible Western-style democracy or a reliable friend of Israel. We may buy periods of quiet, obtain useful concessions or even reach agreements that reduce the danger for years. But none of that necessarily changes the underlying ideology or ambitions of the regime. TRUMP CAN’T LET IRAN TURN A MILITARY DEFEAT INTO A DIPLOMATIC VICTORY Diplomacy with Iran is, in many respects, about buying peace one day at a time while maintaining enough leverage to make renewed aggression unattractive. That leverage must be real. Not another strongly worded statement from Washington or another warning that all options remain on the table. Iran has heard those warnings for decades. Before this war, Iran had developed an extraordinary combination of nuclear expertise, ballistic missiles, drones, underground facilities and regional proxy networks. By June 2025, the International Atomic Energy Agency reported approximately 440.9 kilograms of uranium enriched to 60% purity, technically close to the roughly 90% level associated with weapons-grade material. That did not mean Iran possessed a functioning nuclear weapon, but it demonstrated how far its enrichment program had advanced. Its missiles could reach Israel and American installations throughout the region. Its Shahed drones were being used by Russia against Ukraine. Its scientists and military planners had spent decades developing the ability to manufacture, conceal and replenish these capabilities. AFTER 47 YEARS OF CONFRONTING IRAN, DOES AMERICA HAVE A STRATEGY FOR ENDING THIS WAR? The original nuclear agreement, the JCPOA, should have taught us an important lesson. Iran accepted temporary restrictions but retained the scientific expertise, industrial infrastructure and technical capacity to rebuild its nuclear program. When those restrictions unraveled, Tehran demonstrated how rapidly it could advance toward weapons-grade enrichment. Meanwhile, the International Atomic Energy Agency uncovered undeclared nuclear material and activities that raised serious questions about Iran’s transparency. The lesson is not complicated: an agreement that slows a dangerous program is not the same as one that permanently eliminates the threat. We cannot afford to confuse a diplomatic document with a durable security arrangement. Had we never confronted Iran militarily, those capabilities could have continued to grow. Iran might eventually have been able to choose the timing and circumstances of a confrontation rather than leaving that initiative to us. Now we have acted. We have paid the price, accepted the risks and crossed the threshold into direct military confrontation. What would be the point of all that if we simply allowed Iran to rebuild? TRUMP PUSHED IRAN TO THE BRINK — BUT DID WE WIN ANYTHING THAT LASTS? Imagine two Middle Easts five years from now. In the first, Washington announces that the war is over. The military goes home. The pressure comes off. Oil prices decline, at least initially, and everyone celebrates. Meanwhile, Iran’s surviving leadership quietly begins rebuilding its missile factories, drone production facilities and underground nuclear infrastructure. Money starts flowing again to Hezbollah, Hamas, the Houthis and other armed groups. The regime has learned valuable lessons about our weapons, intelligence capabilities and, perhaps most importantly, our political patience. Five years later, we face an Iran that is better prepared, more deeply entrenched and potentially more dangerous than the one we confronted. IRAN’S DEEPEST WEAKNESS IS GETTING EXPOSED THROUGH AMERICA’S MAXIMUM PRESSURE CAMPAIGN Now imagine the second Middle East. We continue negotiating, but also maintain tough financial sanctions, lawful maritime pressure and an active military component. When intelligence establishes that Iran is restoring threatening military capabilities, and force is legally justified, we retain the ability and willingness to act. Missile and drone manufacturing remain constrained. Nuclear reconstruction is subject to verification and credible consequences. Iran’s ability to finance and arm its proxies is diminished. The regime may never surrender or abandon its ideology, but its capacity to turn that ideology into military action is substantially reduced. That is what I mean by putting Iran in a box. We do not need to occupy the country, install a new government or demand a surrender ceremony in Tehran. We need to make it exceedingly difficult for the regime to rebuild the capabilities that threaten America, Israel and our allies. TRUMP’S PRESSURE CAMPAIGN HAS IRAN REELING. AMERICA CAN’T HESITATE NOW Consider Pickaxe Mountain, the deeply buried complex near Natanz. Analysts have documented extensive construction and hardening activity, although its operational purpose has not been conclusively established. Iran’s investment in facilities designed to withstand attack should remind us that destroying existing infrastructure is not the same as preventing reconstruction. We need inspections, intelligence and a willingness to enforce meaningful restrictions. We should not assume that every construction project is a legitimate military target, but neither should we wait passively while a demonstrable threat is reconstituted. Our strategy needs three legs, and all three must operate simultaneously. IRAN LOSES KEY ECONOMIC LIFELINE IN MIDDLE EAST THAT TRUMP'S SANCTIONS COULDN'T REACH AS DEADLOCK PERSISTS The first is diplomacy. We should negotiate continuously and seriously, offering Iran a verifiable path toward reduced isolation in exchange for meaningful nuclear restrictions, an end to threatening regional activities and respect for freedom of navigation. The second is economic pressure. Financial sanctions, restrictions on weapons-related technology and lawful enforcement around the Strait of Hormuz must continue to limit the regime’s ability to finance military reconstruction and its proxy networks. The third is military force. And I do not mean merely threatening to use it someday. I mean the sustained, periodic and deliberate use of kinetic force against legitimate military targets, guided by intelligence and justified under international and domestic law. Iran must understand that rebuilding its threatening military capabilities is not a risk-free exercise undertaken between rounds of diplomacy. When renewed military activity presents a demonstrable threat and the legal conditions for force are met, America must be prepared to act repeatedly, not simply issue another warning. This is not about launching another full-scale war every six months. It is about ensuring that military pressure remains an active instrument of our strategy, operating alongside diplomacy and sanctions rather than waiting for both to fail. Every operation must have a defined military objective, comply with the law of armed conflict and account for the risks of escalation. The regime should never be allowed to mistake a pause in American military operations for permission to rebuild the capabilities we went to war to destroy. TRUMP KEEPS NEGOTIATING WHILE IRAN PLAYS THE LONG GAME AMERICA KEEPS MISSING This is where I part company with those who believe that once the shooting stops, diplomacy and sanctions alone will finish the job. We have spent decades testing the limits of warnings, sanctions and negotiations. We should be realistic about both their value and their limitations. Congress is understandably worried about gasoline and fertilizer prices. So am I. The Strait of Hormuz is critical to global energy markets, and disruptions affect farmers, businesses and families far beyond the Middle East. But this is not a choice between war and expensive gasoline on one side and peace and cheap gasoline on the other. That is a dangerously simplistic way to evaluate national security. An Iran capable of threatening Gulf oil facilities, international shipping and neighboring countries can impose enormous economic costs whenever it chooses. A nuclear-armed Iran, or one able to approach that capability rapidly, would present an even greater strategic challenge. Continued military operations also carry costs and risks, including retaliation and prolonged economic disruption. Those risks must be weighed carefully. But a few months of lower gasoline prices would be a poor bargain if the result were a more dangerous Iran five years from now. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION The administration has not done nearly enough to explain this to Congress or the American people. We hear about destroyed targets and military victories, negotiations and the possibility of ending the war. What we hear far less about is what happens afterward. How do we prevent Iran from rebuilding? What constitutes a verifiable agreement? What are the consequences if Tehran cheats? And what does victory actually look like? Victory does not mean Iran becomes Switzerland. It does not mean the mullahs embrace Western values or suddenly recognize Israel. It means Iran cannot acquire nuclear weapons, cannot readily rebuild threatening missile and drone capabilities, cannot finance its regional proxies at previous levels and cannot routinely hold international commerce hostage. It means that even if the regime remains hostile, its ability to act on that hostility is significantly constrained. We have poked the bear. It is wounded, angry and dangerous. We should expect it to look for opportunities to recover and lash out. The answer is not to assume that a wounded bear has suddenly become tame, nor is it to fight without limits or an endgame. The answer is to maintain a strategy that keeps the threat contained while creating opportunities for a verifiable diplomatic settlement. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP We crossed the Rubicon when we decided to use military force against Iran. We cannot undo that decision, and we should not squander the advantage it created. Diplomacy, economic pressure and active military enforcement must work together. None is sufficient by itself. We do not need to fight forever. But we cannot simply stop fighting, declare victory and hope Iran plays nice. We have come too far, spent too much and accepted too many risks to confuse a pause in the shooting with the end of the threat. CLICK HERE TO READ MORE FROM GORDON SONDLAND

articles.title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns after affair with suspected Chinese spy
articles.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has resigned in the wake of reports that he had multiple extramarital relationships.
articles.body: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has resigned following reports that he had multiple extramarital relationships, including one with a suspected agent of China and another with an executive who reported to him — a stunning turn of events for the head of a company at the heart of the global AI investment boom. Colette Kress, the company’s chief financial officer, will become interim CEO, Nvidia’s board said in a statement. Nvidia shares plunged more than 11% after the board’s announcement. A company spokesperson clarified that Huang will not be working with NVIDIA in any capacity going forward. The company also named its first chairman. That role will be filled by Harvey Jones, who is a former CEO of major chip company Synopsys. The addition of a chairman is a major governance overhaul at the company that for decades relied solely on Huang. Nvidia’s board met Wednesday night to address Huang’s future at the company, a source familiar with the matter told NBC News, adding that the White House was aware of the meeting. Huang, 63, co-founded Nvidia in the early 1990s, and led the company’s meteoric rise amid the AI boom of the past several years. “I believe deeply in this company and in its future,” Kress wrote in her first email to Nvidia employees as interim CEO. “The Board, Estaff and I recognize that this has been an extraordinarily difficult period and I want you to know how grateful we are for your resilience, professionalism and continued dedication. Thank you.” In a separate note to the company’s workforce, newly-installed chairman Harvey Jones wrote, “The Board takes seriously our duty as stewards of this great company.” In Collette Kress, Nvidia’s board selected a steady hand to steer the company in its most uncertain period ever. Kress has been the company’s chief financial officer since 2013. She is a familiar face to Wall Street, regularly appearing at conferences and discussing the intricacies of the company’s sprawling operations. Before Nvidia, Kress worked at Cisco, another major technology company, and Microsoft. Huang long leaned on Kress during financial conferences and the company’s earnings calls to debrief the investing public about the latest developments with the company’s operations. Nvidia’s board said that it would search for a permanent CEO and consider internal and external candidates. Trump weighed in on the search for a permanent CEO shortly after Nvidia’s announcement, saying that Apple executive chair Tim Cook should take the role. “A Legend replaces a Legend!” Trump wrote. Cook only became Apple’s executive chair on September 1, and did not appear to have plans to leave any time soon. Kress’ ascension to the CEO suite comes after the second largest public company in the world was hit with multiple scandals involving its founder. On Wednesday, The New York Times, citing five people who worked at Nvidia, reported that Huang had an extramarital relationship with a married healthcare executive who reported to him, which appears to run afoul of Nvidia’s code of conduct. NBC News has not independently verified the claims. Nvidia and the executive did not respond to multiple requests for comment Wednesday about the Times’ report. The report concerning the alleged relationship followed reports that Huang had an affair with Alice Huang, a businesswoman believed to be a spy for China. The two Huangs are not related. Secretary of State Marco Rubio circulated a memo to officials in the Trump administration this spring outlining how U.S. intelligence showed that Huang was in a romantic relationship with a business executive who was an asset of China’s spy service, according to a person familiar with Nvidia and a former national security official with knowledge of the matter. The New York Times and the Financial Times, citing people familiar with the matter, first reported on the memo last week. Alice Huang held a senior position at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that was buying advanced chips from Nvidia. Megaspeed and other related firms remain under U.S. criminal investigation of allegations they smuggled American-made chips into China. Alice Huang’s precise role and relationship with China’s spy service is unclear. It is possible she was not a career spy for China’s spy agency, the Ministry of State Security, but was asked to cooperate and share information based on her access to Jensen Huang, according to the former national security official. The concerns about the Nvidia CEO’s extramarital activity added to worries about Nvidia chips being smuggled or illegally accessed by Chinese AI companies. Nvidia has said that it follows U.S. export laws. On Sunday, Nvidia’s board announced it was investigating whether Huang had fallen victim to a foreign intelligence plot. It said Tuesday that it had hired a former acting U.S. attorney and his law firm to conduct the investigation. Huang apologized in a memo to employees and said he supported the independent investigation. “I was unfaithful to my wife,” he wrote. “My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.” Multiple Washington officials have called for greater scrutiny of Nvidia and for Huang to testify about his relationship with the suspected Chinese agent in the wake of the reports. China has denied the allegations, calling them “purely unsubstantiated and directed at smearing China.” Even before Wednesday’s Times report, Nvidia shares had plunged 11% this week, wiping out nearly $500 billion in paper value. Huang’s departure leaves a host of unknowns at the company, the valuation of which has soared to more than $1 trillion amid insatiable demand for its GPU chips. Those specialized processors underpin the AI applications that have powered the stock market and economic growth writ large to new heights. For years, Huang has effectively been the chief ambassador for the artificial intelligence industry, appearing regularly alongside heads of state and other CEOs as the industry spends trillions of dollars investing and building AI models and data centers. Nvidia acknowledged Huang’s contributions to the sector in its Thursday announcement. “Jensen’s contributions to NVIDIA are profound,” a statement said. “The Board and the company thank Jensen for his immeasurable contributions to the company and the industry.” After coming up with the idea for Nvidia at a Denny’s restaurant in Silicon Valley with co-founders Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem, Huang built the company into a $4 trillion global chip behemoth over the following 30-plus years. Before Wednesday’s report of a second affair, many high-profile figures across Silicon Valley, Wall Street and Washington had come to Huang’s defense. President Donald Trump told reporters Sunday that Huang had “done an amazing job for our country.” “I think he’s an honorable guy,” Trump said. “I think he probably has an excuse for it. You have to hear it.” Shaun Maguire, a partner at the venture capital group Sequoia, said on X that Huang is “one of the greatest entrepreneurs of this generation,” adding that “two mistakes don’t make a right, and I believe Jensen is irreplaceable for America’s AI leadership.” SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk responded under Maguire’s post, writing: “I agree.” Before the decision, Musk said in a response to a post Wednesday night that it “would be an honor” to hire Huang.

articles.title: ‘No war, no peace’: Can Iran break the deadlock with the US?
articles.summary: Sustainable stalemate or slow-motion strangulation? The current ‘equilibrium’ is inherently unstable, experts say.
articles.body:
As the United States-Iran war drags on and talks remain stalled, Tehran is determined to move beyond a state of “no war and no peace”, parliament speaker and chief negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf has told Al Jazeera.

Iran continues to assert control over which vessels may pass through the Strait of Hormuz, where attacks on tankers taking “unauthorised” routes have disrupted shipping.

Ghalibaf says Tehran remains open to a deal with the US to agree a ceasefire and the reopening of the strait, and has been waiting for Washington to respond to its terms for this to happen. “The ball is now in the American court,” he said.

Faced with the prospect of restarting an unpopular war or making concessions to Iran in order to secure a deal, experts say US President Donald Trump has for now chosen to ratchet up economic pressure. To this end, Washington has tightened sanctions, maintained its blockade on Iranian ports and announced an operation that Trump says will cut off overland routes Iran uses to transport advanced weapons and technology.

For now, full-scale fighting remains on hold, but a formal peace deal is still out of reach, with a fragile stalemate that may not hold for long, experts say.

“The current equilibrium is inherently unstable,” Ali Vaez, deputy programme director for the Middle East and North Africa at the International Crisis Group, told Al Jazeera. “Because what Washington considers a sustainable stalemate, Tehran sees as a slow-motion strangulation. Both sides are banking on the other’s pain threshold being lower than their own.”

Tehran has laid down seven conditions before it will agree to a ceasefire and the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, then restart peace talks through a Qatari mediator, and has been waiting for an official US response to its demands. They include the lifting of the US naval blockade on Iranian ports, sanctions relief, releasing frozen Iranian funds, ending hostilities on all fronts and formally declaring the war over.

Ghalibaf said these conditions had already formed part of the memorandum of understanding (MoU) reached with the US in Islamabad in June and must be implemented before Iran will re-enter negotiations with the US.

But Tehran’s push for a deal reflects the pressure the blockade and sanctions are placing on its economy, analysts say. The longer that pressure lasts, the harder it may become for Iran’s leaders to agree to terms they may struggle to defend at home.

“Iran wants relief from the siege, but after paying such a heavy price … its leaders cannot afford a settlement that looks like surrender,” Vaez said. “The more Washington demands capitulation, the more elusive a deal becomes.”

But there are still signs of movement. Qatar said on Tuesday it was “working tirelessly” to resolve the crisis and that both sides had made positive statements about diplomacy. A day earlier, after hosting Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani at the White House, Trump said there was “momentum towards the end of this conflict”. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, however, has described Iran’s demands as “unacceptable”.

Gerd Nonneman, a professor of international relations and Gulf studies at Georgetown University in Qatar, told Al Jazeera that the cost of keeping up this pressure could narrow Washington’s room for manoeuvre.

“The US side may very temporarily think the status quo is preferable to making significant concessions now, but that will never be a sustainable strategy as it is prohibitively expensive, both in terms of overall economic effects and of the cost of the military operation,” he said.

Iran’s main source of leverage in the standoff is the Strait of Hormuz, analysts say. By seeking to dictate which ships can pass and which routes they can take, Tehran can raise the cost of the stalemate for Washington and its Gulf partners. Ghalibaf told Al Jazeera the waterway would “never return” to its pre-war status.

That leverage was on display last weekend, when shipping slowed sharply following attacks on tankers. Just five commodity vessels crossed on Saturday, November 7, while trade intelligence firm Kpler recorded none on Sunday, November 8. That compares with 31 crossings over the previous weekend, the Reuters news agency reported, citing the firm’s ship-tracking data.

In a statement carried by the Tasnim news agency, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said a “massive explosion” on Wednesday night brought two supertankers to a standstill as they travelled along a route it said was unauthorised. The IRGC said the vessels were carrying more than four million barrels of oil between them.

Analysts say intermittent attacks on tankers allow Iran to destabilise shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, preserving its main source of leverage over Washington.

“Washington has the luxury of waiting, but it does not have the luxury of deciding how Tehran behaves while it waits,” Vaez said. “The paradox is that the more effective America’s pressure campaign becomes, the greater Iran’s incentive to break the impasse by force.”

Trump’s advisers are reportedly divided over what to do next. Rubio has argued that the economic pressure campaign is working, while US Vice President JD Vance has pushed for a negotiated deal, according to Axios. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, CIA Director John Ratcliffe and Trump’s adviser and son-in-law Jared Kushner have backed maintaining economic pressure, the outlet reported.

“While neither would like to return to a state of war, I think the US is slightly more keen than Iran on the current stalemate, as a result of the economic pressure inflicted by the naval blockade,” Albert Vidal, of the International Institute for Strategic Studies, told Al Jazeera.

The US midterm elections last week could also affect Trump’s calculations. When the new Congress takes office in January, Democrats could use their newfound control over spending to make it harder for the administration to sustain military operations, Vidal said.

“At the same time, the Trump administration’s window to conduct major operations may be closing, too, as Democrats might choose to use the power of the purse in the new Congress in January,” he said.

Vidal said shortages of ballistic missile interceptors could push Washington to limit any renewed fighting.

Iran, meanwhile, has signalled that it may retaliate against civilian infrastructure as well as US military bases in the region, he said. A decision to resume hostilities could therefore draw Gulf countries further into a war whose economic and human costs they are already bearing.

“The tragedy is that both sides know how to start another round of hostilities, but neither knows how to control or end it,” Vaez said.

articles.title: Nonprofit offers veterans second career through commercial drone pilot training
articles.summary: After the military, some veterans are left wondering what's next? Nonprofit organization Vets to Drones is helping them take on a new path by becoming certified drone pilots.
articles.body: Each year more than 200,000 service members leave active duty and return to civilian life, but the transition is not the easiest. Vets to Drones, a nonprofit that helps veterans gain training and experience in the drone industry, is trying to change that by helping veterans find a second career after leaving the military. Kickstarted by Marine Corps veteran Chris Lewis after a recent trip to California aiding in wildfire mitigation, Lewis knew what it was like to leave the military and search for a new path forward. "I ended up right back in the civilian world, searching for answers I guess," Lewis said. AI FIREFIGHTING DRONES TAKE AIM AT WILDFIRES Lewis handled drones for a short time while deployed, but realized there's a bigger future with unmanned aircraft systems. He started Vets to Drones with a fellow Marine who died in 2022, which ultimately pushed him even harder to help other veterans through the organization. He believes the drone industry is a true fit for military members looking to enter the civilian workforce, adding that many of their field and infantry skills cross over seamlessly. Vets to Drones has become a pipeline for the drone workforce, while bringing a new sense of purpose and community to veterans. MARINE REFUSES TO BACK DOWN IN 16-YEAR FIGHT When Marine veteran Dusty Lopez left the military, he got into disaster recovery and insurance, then started his own business in insurance claims and assessment. Lopez came into contact with Vets to Drones at an event after clients asked him if he had drones to help with some of the jobs. That meeting led to a partnership with his company, Struction Solutions. "I still live by the Marine Corps motto: honor, courage, and commitment," Lopez said, adding that the branch helped him shape his career outside the military. Now, Lopez has nearly a dozen drones for different jobs. One hefty drone, typically used by law enforcement or first responders for security over watch, is tethered and can stay in the air for days at a time. PENTAGON CONSOLIDATES DRONE OVERSIGHT Veterans across the country train under Vets to Drones, then become FAA Commercial Drone certified, which leads them to jobs in several sectors. Through the organization, veterans have participated in search and rescue, helped farmers, guided first responders during natural disasters and provided assistance for security operations, according to Lewis. In the aftermath of Hurricane Ida's landfall in Louisiana, Lewis said they created a 360 view similar to Google Earth, but "from the sky with the drone." "It's [an] incredible feeling when I get that phone call [that] says, 'hey, man, thank you. I had no idea this was a thing. And now I'm able to feed my family with this new skill,'" Lewis said.

articles.title: Spain approves housing reforms after nationwide strike over costs
articles.summary: Spanish parliament passes new laws limiting evictions but their duration depends on the upcoming snap election outcome.
articles.body:
The Spanish parliament has passed measures to limit evictions and real estate speculation in an attempt to make housing more affordable, a day after a nationwide general strike over the country’s housing crisis.

Spain’s interim lower house of parliament ratified the housing measures on Thursday; however, their duration will depend on the outcome of a snap election scheduled later in November.

The leading opposition party, the conservative Popular Party, has said that it will repeal the measures of the left-wing government if it takes power, which polls indicate could happen.

Large demonstrations over unaffordable housing swept the country in September when televised images of the eviction of 87-year-old Maria del Carmen Abascal , known as Maricarmen, from her home, shocked many Spaniards.

Protest camps sprang up in several cities, the largest in Madrid’s emblematic Puerta del Sol square. Maricarmen’s subsequent death in October caused national uproar, prompting Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez’s minority government to rush to present two decrees.

Sanchez called the general election, which had been scheduled for 2027, in response to the parliament’s failure to pass the decrees that included greater protection for tenants against evictions and the automatic renewal of tenant contracts.

The Popular Party and other conservative parties aligned to reject the measures, saying the laws would negatively affect the housing market, and proposed a building spree as the solution to the crisis.

On Wednesday, hundreds of thousands of Spaniards took to the streets in a 24-hour walkout over soaring rents and the high cost of living that the main unions called after the decrees were blocked.

Sanchez introduced another two decrees that were almost identical to the rejected ones. They were presented to a smaller parliamentary council on Thursday, giving the government a better chance of passing the laws.

The first decree passed in a 35–34 vote and includes a measure extending protections against evictions for tenants deemed by social services to be in a precarious financial or social position, as long as regional authorities cannot offer them an alternative residence.

Another measure attempted to reduce real estate speculation by stopping any company involved in the real estate market from buying properties for less than 70 percent of their value.

However, it was rejected 34-35 after the centre-right Basque party voted with the right-wing bloc after having supported the other decree, on grounds that the measure could lead homeowners to withdraw their properties from the rental market, triggering a drop in supply and even higher prices.

articles.title: Guernsey library will not remove David Walliams books
articles.summary: Guille-Alles Library says it would "protect people's freedom to read what they want to read".
articles.body:
A Guernsey library will continue to loan out books authored by David Walliams after allegations of sexual misconduct were made against him.

Guille-Alles Library, in St Peter Port, said literature should remain available to readers unless the content was illegal.

A spokesperson said "we recognise this is a sensitive and complex issue" but added "we take seriously our responsibility to protect people's freedom to read what they want to read".

Reports by ITV News and the Guardian on Tuesday alleged Walliams had been accused of sexual misconduct by several women. He denies all of the allegations against him.

The library spokesperson said: "As a public library, we follow established professional and ethical principles in deciding which books to include in our collection.

"The starting point is that books should remain available to readers unless the content of those books is illegal."

In his statement to ITV News and the Guardian, Walliams said: "Looking back, I realise that at times I behaved thoughtlessly towards other people I had casual sexual relationships with.

"I realise I did not always take people's feelings properly into account. That is something I regret. And whilst a power imbalance is inevitable when one party is famous, abusing that power is something else entirely and it is something that I never did.

"I am not a sexual predator. I have not broken the law, but I am devastated that some of the women I met 10 to 20 years ago have now expressed hurt or anger towards me."

articles.title: UK court finds two Iranian men guilty of spying for Iran
articles.summary: The pair were promised rewards to send intelligence back to Iran, while one was prepared to commit a ‘violent attack’.
articles.body:
Two Iranian men have been found guilty of spying for Tehran by a court in the United Kingdom after being accused of conducting surveillance on several people, including journalists for a Persian-language broadcaster in London.

Mostafa Sepahvand, 41, and Farhad Javadi Manesh, 46, were convicted on Thursday following a six-week trial at Woolwich Crown Court in south London for engaging in conduct likely to assist Iran’s intelligence service in a bid to inflict violence on “subjects” in the UK .

These included journalists for Iran International, Mojtaba Pourmohsen and Kambiz Hosseini, and a founding member of UK Lawyers for Israel, Jonathan Turner. Iran International is banned by the government in Tehran.

A third defendant, Shapoor Qalehali Khani Noori, 57, was acquitted on all charges.

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) was outlawed by the UK in July under new powers to counteract state threats, with penalties of up to 14 years in prison for anyone convicted of supporting or assisting the organisation.

“This was a calculated operation to spy on those critical of the Iranian regime,” Frank Ferguson, chief prosecutor for the Crown Prosecution Service’s special crime and counterterrorism division, told reporters.

He said the pair were promised rewards to send intelligence back to Iran, while Sepahvand was willing to go beyond surveillance to commit a “violent attack” against at least one of the targets.

London’s Metropolitan Police said this was the fourth case in recent years involving direct threats to Iranian journalists in the UK and that it is “working hard to keep them safe”.

“The threat from hostile states to the UK is increasing and Iran continues to adapt its approach to using ‘proxies’,” said Vicki Evans, deputy assistant commissioner at the Met.

“We have seen examples where people who fly into the country to carry out criminal activity and then leave shortly afterwards, others where they use British nationals or, in this case, Iranian nationals with settled immigration status,” she added.

Sepahvand and Manesh were accused of visiting addresses linked to their targets, taking photos and videos and using platforms such as ChatGPT to research them online.

The pair will be sentenced at London’s Central Criminal Court, better known as the Old Bailey, on December 17.

articles.title: Senator Tom Cotton urges Trump admin to ban Chinese chipmaker CXMT from US market over security concerns
articles.summary: Senator Tom Cotton demands the Trump administration to restrict Chinese memory chipmaker CXMT due to concerns over national security and economic impact, urging for its addition to the Entity List.
articles.body: US Senator Tom Cotton has urged the Trump administration to impose tighter restrictions on Chinese memory chip manufacturer ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT), arguing that the company's growing presence in the global market could threaten American economic and military interests.In a letter sent on Thursday to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, which was obtained by CNBC, the Republican senator from Arkansas asked the department to add CXMT to the Bureau of Industry and Security's Entity List. Such a designation would significantly restrict the company's access to US technology and limit American businesses' ability to conduct transactions with it.“CXMT, one of Communist China’s national memory chip champions, poses a growing risk to our economic prosperity and military superiority,” Cotton wrote. He urged the administration to prevent the Chinese manufacturer from gaining a stronger foothold in the global market.CXMT is the world's fourth-largest producer of dynamic random-access memory (DRAM), which is used in computers, smartphones and other electronic devices, according to Counterpoint Research.Cotton's request comes as CXMT expands its position in the memory chip market. Its share of global DRAM revenue increased from 4% in the second quarter of 2025 to 10% in the same quarter of 2026, according to Counterpoint data cited by CNBC.The company is already named on the US Department of Defense's 1260H list, which identifies Chinese companies with links to Beijing's military. However, this listing does not impose the same restrictions on American businesses as the Commerce Department's Entity List.Cotton also raised concerns about CXMT's efforts to enter the high-bandwidth memory (HBM) market, which supplies advanced memory chips used in artificial intelligence infrastructure.“[CXMT’s] decision to move forward in less than ideal conditions highlights both Communist China’s desperation for chips and manufacturing struggles without advanced equipment and knowledge,” he wrote.He called for further measures to restrict the company's access to financial and technological resources, arguing that these could strengthen its supply chain and undermine American growth.“More can be done to ensure that CXMT is cut off from the financial and technological resources that aid its supply chain and undercut American growth,” Cotton wrote.You use AI every day. articles.title: Why are there so many security incidents linked to US military in Britain?
articles.summary: A string of recent security incidents at UK military bases used by the United States have forced Washington to hastily relocate several of its aircraft and upgrade the threat level facing some of its troops.
articles.body: A string of recent security incidents at UK military bases used by the United States have forced Washington to hastily relocate several of its aircraft and upgrade the threat level facing some of its troops. On two occasions, once in October and once in November, the US has moved aircraft following threats that officials said emanated from Iran. And in a separate October incident, two Latvian men were arrested inside another Royal Air Force (RAF) base used by US personnel. The frequency of the incidents indicates both the risks inherent in the United Kingdom’s decision to allow US forces to launch defensive strikes against Iran from its airbases, and the country’s strategic significance as a host for expensive US aircraft that make for attractive targets. Britain’s government insists its bases remain secure and says it has heightened security measures across its sites. So, how unusual are these incidents, and why do they seem to be concentrated in the UK? Are there more US troops in the UK than elsewhere? No. About 12,300 US military and defense personnel are stationed in the UK, according to the British government in March, but far more are based in Germany where the US European Command is headquartered. Italy hosts about the same number of American troops as the UK. How important are UK bases to the US military? The UK may not have the highest number of American troops stationed on its soil, but its bases are of enormous strategic importance, often hosting extremely expensive US aircraft. RAF Mildenhall is the US’ only permanent home in Europe for its refueling aircraft, providing critical support that allows US forces to deploy quickly anywhere in the world. Flight tracking data analyzed by CNN shows that 10 US refueling aircraft were relocated away from the base on Monday following a threat from Iran that was deemed credible, according to a person familiar with the intelligence which prompted the evacuation. The source declined to detail the nature of the threat to the base but said that the US intelligence community has in recent weeks picked up a wide range of “varied, extensive, and specific” plots being discussed by the Iranians against American targets. RAF Fairford, which was targeted in September, holds similar strategic significance. Its long runway means it is one of the few US bases in Europe capable of handling all three types of long-range bombers operated by the US Air Force. Importantly, the US has used Fairford to carry out strikes on Iranian missile sites used to attack ships in the Strait of Hormuz, meaning that US B-1 bombers have been stationed there. That made it a prime target for the failed plot, which was directed by the commander of an Iranian terrorist proxy group from his imprisonment in New York, US federal prosecutors alleged in a new indictment on Tuesday. The plan involved using vans filled with fuel as vehicle-borne improvised explosive devices, multiple people briefed on the matter told CNN. As well as targeting US assets, another key aim for Iran in its external attacks has always been to weaken relationships among the US and its allies, said Louise Kettle, a professor at Nottingham University who studies British-Iranian relations. In these cases, “it is about weakening relationships between the US, the UK and Israel,” she told CNN. Are security threats in Britain more acute? In the months after the US and Israel first launched strikes against Iran, the threat the Islamic Republic poses to the UK has shifted. It has attempted to expand its hybrid operations and altered its strategy to “come at harder targets, like military sites,” according to MI5 chief Ken McCallum. That mirrors a wider change in Iran’s strategic approach as its traditional policy of maintaining a “forward defense pattern” through its proxy groups across the Middle East has crumbled, Kettle said. “Not only has the UK changed its approach by allowing the US to use the bases, not only has the global context changed because the US is at war with Iran, but Iran’s strategic capabilities have also changed, and therefore you must expect them to change their strategy,” she added. Just last week, Iranian state-linked media Hamshahri threatened other European bases, including some situated in Germany, Italy and Greece. “We’ll see what happens,” the newspaper’s front page warned, complete with a mocked-up map of Europe and red pins marking each base it threatened. McCallum said the Fairford incident was “not unique,” adding that “there have been other examples, not just in the UK, but around the world,” without providing further details. Still, McCallum noted that Iran’s capabilities when operating far outside its borders are mostly limited to subcontracting “criminal proxies.” That limits its capabilities to only the “sophistication level of those criminals,” he added, saying that the police and intelligence services can currently deal with these threats “pretty capably.” In the UK, the threats have primarily manifested as attacks on the Jewish community, dissident journalists and against military bases. But they can take different forms in different countries. France, which has no permanent US troops to target but took part in “defensive” operations against Iran, blamed the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps on Monday for last month’s supermarket fridge cyberattack that spoiled produce at around 700 retailers, a claim Tehran says is “baseless and hostile.” How unusual are these types of incidents? When British police were alerted to three suspicious vehicles driving toward Fairford in September, the incident sparked huge international attention for its unusualness. But military bases, by their very nature, are always targets for an attack. “If you host another country who are fighting someone else, (bases) naturally becomes a target for the country they are fighting,” noted Kettle. “So, this isn’t unique to the UK, it’s a standard part of warfare.” Back in November 2024, several bases across Europe which host US troops reported seeing small drones flying over them. They were never officially identified but a report from the International Institute of Strategic Studies, a security think-tank, assessed they could have been part of a campaign directed by Moscow. Security at British bases is “layered and intelligence-led,” the country’s minister for defense readiness, Luke Pollard, said Thursday. “It combines physical protection, access controls, surveillance, policing, guarding, aerial monitoring, and counter-drone capabilities. We do not rely on any one single measure.”
